title: Measuring Feature Impact (TARS)
intro: Measure a feature against the users who have the problem it solves — not all users.

learn.title: The four steps
learn.text:
**T · Target** — the percentage of users who actually have the problem
**A · Adoption** — the percentage of that target who meaningfully use it
**R · Retention** — the percentage of adopters who come back
**S · Satisfaction** — Customer Effort Score, asked only of retained users

TARS deliberately leaves out conversion: too many non-design factors move it.

options: Too many non-design factors move it
It is hard to measure accurately
try.explain: Pricing, marketing and seasonality all move conversion.

learn.title: Reading the numbers
learn.text:
**Adoption** above ~60% suggests the feature solves a real problem. Below ~20% often means easy workarounds exist, or the feature isn't discoverable.

**Retention** above 50% signals high strategic importance; 25–35% medium; 10–20% low.

A niche feature used by 50–75% of its 10% audience can be a success. The denominator is what makes that judgement possible.

try.q: Adoption is 15% of the target audience. What are the likely explanations?
options: The target was estimated too narrowly
try.explain: Below ~20% is the warning band. Or poor discoverability.

learn.title: Counting the right things
learn.text:
**Target:** estimate from similar features. Usage of the feature itself is not the audience — that's circular.

**Adoption:** count value signals — exports shared, filters used — not clicks or session time.

**Satisfaction:** Customer Effort Score, from “much harder” to “much easier than expected”, asked of people who kept using it.

try.q: What is wrong with using the feature's own usage to define the target audience?

test.q: What does the T stand for?
test.explain: The users who have the problem the feature solves.

options: A click on the menu item

test.q: Who is asked the satisfaction question?
test.explain: CES, from people who kept using it.

test.q: Can a feature used by 10% of users be a success?
options: Yes, if it reaches most of its target
